implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library ships the predicate form as extension functions on the mutable collection interfaces: MutableList.removeAll(predicate) 'removes all elements from this MutableList that match the given predicate' and retainAll(predicate) keeps the ones that match, both returning whether anything changed; internally the collection is walked once and elements are removed through its iterator, with an index-based variant for RandomAccess lists. That is the whole idiom - the C++ algorithm-plus-erase pair has no counterpart because the receiver owns both the scan and the size change. The by-value overloads (removeAll(elements: Collection<T>)) and MutableSet/HashSet removal cover the membership cases, while read-only and immutable lists require the copy-out form (filter/filterNot) because they expose no mutation at all.
pitfalls: Predicate polarity is inverted between the two functions: removeAll drops the elements the lambda accepts while retainAll keeps them, so copying a block between the two is a silent logic flip.

The extension lives on MutableList/MutableIterable: a read-only List does not compile (good), and casting a read-only view backed by Arrays.asList or Collections.unmodifiableList to MutableList throws UnsupportedOperationException at the first removal.
Concurrent modification: mutating the list inside the predicate, or removing by index while iterating, throws ConcurrentModificationException or shifts indices out from under the loop.
On a MutableSet/HashSet removal is per entry and unordered, so the ordering guarantee and the compaction cost model both stop applying.
